front: What key assumption is built into the Galilean transformations?
back: Time is absolute: $t' = t$ for all observers, so time intervals and lengths are the same in every frame.

front: Why can’t $u' = u - v$ be applied to light?
back: It would give light different speeds in different frames, contradicting the second postulate (and experiment). It is only valid for $v \ll c$.

front: In $x' = x - vt$, what exactly is $v$?
back: The velocity of frame S′ **measured in** S (along +x). Getting this sign wrong flips the answer.
$\gamma \ge 1$ always: $\gamma \approx 1$ for $v \ll c$, and $\gamma \to \infty$ as $v \to c$ — so no massive object can reach $c$.

front: What is the physical significance of the $vx/c^2$ term in $t'$?
back: It makes simultaneity relative: events with the same $t$ but different $x$ in S have different $t'$ in S′.
Two events at different places that are simultaneous in one inertial frame are generally **not** simultaneous in another frame moving relative to it.

front: A clock moves at 0.8c past you. It ticks 1.00 s in its own frame. What interval do you measure?
back: $\gamma = 1.67$, so $\Delta t = \gamma\Delta t_0 \approx 1.67$ s — moving clocks run slow.

front: In which directions is a moving object contracted?
back: Only along its direction of motion. Perpendicular lengths are unchanged.

front: Name quantities all inertial observers agree on.
back: The speed of light $c$, the space–time interval $(\Delta s)^2$, proper time and proper length.

front: How can you check the relativistic velocity addition formula with light?
back: Put $u = c$: $u' = \dfrac{c - v}{1 - v/c} = c$ — light has speed $c$ in every frame, as the second postulate demands.

front: How are the axes of frame S′ (speed $v$) drawn on a space–time diagram of S?
back: The $ct'$ axis is the world line of the S′ origin, at angle θ to $ct$ with $\tan\theta = v/c$. The $x'$ axis is tilted by the same θ from the $x$ axis, towards the 45° light line.

front: How do you read off which events are simultaneous in S′ on a space–time diagram?
back: Events on a line **parallel to the $x'$ axis** have the same $t'$. Read times in S′ by drawing lines parallel to $x'$ to the $ct'$ axis.

front: Why is the vertical axis of a space–time diagram $ct$ rather than $t$?
back: So both axes are in metres and light’s world line is at exactly 45°.
